name: KTTKS

lead: KTTKS is a five-amino-acid peptide, usually attached to a palmitoyl fat chain (Pal-KTTKS) and sold as Matrixyl in anti-wrinkle products since 2000. People use it to smooth fine lines and firm skin.

It is a matrikine, a messenger peptide reported to stimulate extracellular matrix and collagen synthesis in skin cells, and the fat chain is meant to aid penetration. A 12-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled split-face study of 93 women aged 35 to 55 assessed it in photoaged facial skin and reported improvement, and lab work shows it raises collagen production in cultured fibroblasts. Reviewers discuss how well the peptide reaches the dermis.

paras: It is used as a leave-on serum or cream ingredient, typically as part of a daily anti-aging routine. Studies of it ran for around 12 weeks.
The sources reviewed do not report safety problems. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient, not a drug.

angle.text: KTTKS, sold as Matrixyl in palmitoylated form, is a collagen-signalling peptide used in anti-wrinkle skincare. It signals skin cells to make more collagen and matrix, which smooths fine lines. A 93-subject split-face trial studied it, and skin penetration is discussed in the literature.

lead: KTTKS is a pentapeptide (lysine-threonine-threonine-lysine-serine) used in anti-wrinkle skin care, usually in its palmitoylated form, palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (Pal-KTTKS), sold under the trade name Matrixyl. Sederma launched Matrixyl in 2000. It is classed as a matrikine, a messenger peptide that regulates cell activity [1][2].

It was designed as a topical agent to stimulate collagen production. In a 12-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled, split-face study of 93 women aged 35 to 55, pal-KTTKS was assessed for improvement in photoaged facial skin [3]. Laboratory work shows C16-KTTKS stimulates collagen production in human fibroblasts [4]. Questions about how well the peptide penetrates skin are discussed in the literature [5][6].

paras: KTTKS is a cosmetic ingredient aimed at wrinkles and photoaged skin. The 16-carbon palmitoyl chain is intended to help the molecule cross the skin's lipid layers [1].

Wikipedia describes the peptide as activating the synthesis of extracellular matrix macromolecules, linking this to its anti-wrinkle effect [1]. In vitro, C16-KTTKS stimulated collagen production in human dermal and corneal fibroblasts in a concentration-dependent manner, close to the concentration at which it self-assembles into nanotape structures [4]. Related work found KTTKS increased type I collagen and TGF-beta expression in tendon cells [7].

Studies have examined stability and permeation of KTTKS and palmitoyl-KTTKS in skin [6], microneedle-enhanced delivery of cosmeceutical peptides [8], and the argument that skin permeability is a necessary consideration for anti-wrinkle peptide performance [5]. Reviews of topical KTTKS are available [2].

A 12-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled, split-face, left-right randomized study in 93 Caucasian female subjects aged 35 to 55 compared pal-KTTKS-containing formulations with comparators for photoaged facial skin, and was reported as showing improvement [3]. The study design used the peptide's collagen-stimulating rationale [3]. The sources reviewed do not describe independent replication in this summary, and a 2011 review discusses topical KTTKS evidence overall [2].
Matrixyl and related peptides are marketed in cosmetic products. The sources reviewed contain no looksmaxxing community discussion of KTTKS.

timeline.event: Clinical study of pal-KTTKS in photoaged facial skin published [3].
